title: General Concept of Laser
short_intro: LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation, producing a highly directional, coherent, and monochromatic beam of light. Its operation relies on population inversion and optical or electrical pumping within an active medium.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic principles of absorption, spontaneous emission, stimulated emission, Einstein's coefficients, and general characteristics of laser light.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed analysis of population inversion, three-level and four-level laser systems, threshold pumping conditions, spatial and temporal coherence, and cavity resonance modes.

prerequisites: Bohr's atomic model and energy levels
Planck's radiation law and thermal equilibrium
Wave optics, interference, and spatial/temporal coherence

concept_notes.heading: Stimulated Emission and Einstein A & B Coefficients
bullets: Light interaction with matter involves three processes: induced absorption, spontaneous emission, and stimulated emission.

Stimulated emission occurs when an incident photon of energy hν triggers an excited electron to drop to a lower energy state, releasing a photon identical in phase, frequency, polarization, and direction.
Einstein's coefficients A<sub>21</sub>, B<sub>12</sub>, and B<sub>21</sub> quantify the transition rates for spontaneous emission, absorption, and stimulated emission respectively.

concept_notes.heading: Population Inversion and Pumping Mechanisms
bullets: Under thermal equilibrium, the population of lower energy states exceeds higher states according to the Boltzmann distribution.
Population inversion is a non-equilibrium state where the population of a higher energy level (N<sub>2</sub>) exceeds that of a lower level (N<sub>1</sub>), i.e., N<sub>2</sub> > N<sub>1</sub>.
Pumping is the method of exciting atoms from the ground state to higher energy states using optical, electrical, or chemical energy sources to achieve population inversion.

concept_notes.heading: Optical Resonator and Laser Cavity
bullets: An optical cavity consists of two mirrors placed facing each other, one fully reflective and the other partially transmitting, enclosing the active medium.
The cavity provides optical feedback, forcing photons to pass back and forth through the active medium, causing cumulative stimulated emission.
Standing waves are established in the cavity corresponding to specific resonant frequencies whose wavelengths fit an integral multiple of half the cavity length.

concept_notes.heading: Characteristics of Laser Radiation
bullets: Monochromaticity: The emitted light possesses an extremely narrow spectral width due to stimulated transitions between specific atomic energy levels.
Coherence: Photons are in phase with each other, showing high temporal and spatial coherence.
Directionality: The beam exhibits extremely low angular divergence, allowing it to propagate over long distances without significant spreading.

derivations.title: Threshold Condition for Population Inversion
derivations.conditions: Steady-state operation in a laser cavity of length L with mirror reflectivities R<sub>1</sub> and R<sub>2</sub>
steps: Consider a light wave of intensity I making a round trip in the cavity of length L with active medium gain coefficient g<sub>th</sub>.
Account for cavity losses per round trip due to mirror transmission, diffraction, and scattering, represented by absorption coefficient α.
Write the threshold condition for steady-state amplification: R_{1} R_{2} e^{2(g_{th} - alpha)L} = 1.
Take the natural logarithm of both sides to solve for threshold gain g_{th}.
derivations.result: g_{th} = alpha +  rac{1}{2L} lnleft( rac{1}{R_1 R_2}ight)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Energy Level Diagram for Three-Level and Four-Level Lasers
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic energy levels E_0, E_1, E_2, E_3 showing pumping transitions, fast non-radiative decay, and laser transition.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how population inversion is maintained more efficiently in four-level systems due to a lower threshold compared to three-level systems.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently asked in conceptual questions comparing laser efficiency and pumping requirements.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Laser Output Power vs Pumping Current/Power
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve showing near-zero output power up to a critical pumping threshold, followed by a linear rise in output power beyond the threshold.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Identifies the threshold pumping rate required to overcome cavity losses and initiate laser action.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested via graphical interpretation questions in PGT examinations.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the ratio of the rate of spontaneous emission to the rate of stimulated emission for a system in thermal equilibrium at temperature T = 300 K, emitting radiation of wavelength λ = 600 nm.
solution_steps:
Recall the ratio of emission rates: R_{spont} / R_{stim} = A_{21} / [U(
u) B_{21}] = e^{(h
u/kT)} - 1.

Calculate the photon energy h
u: h
u = hc / lambda = (6.63 \times 10^{-34} \text{ J s} \times 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}) / (600 \times 10^{-9} \text{ m}) = 3.315 \times 10^{-19} \text{ J}.
Calculate thermal energy kT: kT = (1.38 \times 10^{-23} \text{ J/K}) \times 300 \text{ K} = 4.14 \times 10^{-21} \text{ J}.

solved_numericals.question: A laser optical cavity has a length L = 30 cm and mirror reflectivities R_1 = 1.0 and R_2 = 0.95. The internal scattering loss coefficient α = 0.02 cm^{-1}. Find the threshold gain coefficient g_{th}.
solution_steps: Convert cavity length to meters or keep in cm consistent with α: L = 30 cm.
Use the threshold gain formula: g_{th} = \alpha + \frac{1}{2L} \ln\left(\frac{1}{R_1 R_2}ight).

solved_numericals.question: Find the longitudinal mode separation (frequency interval Δν) for a He-Ne laser operating at λ = 632.8 nm with a cavity length L = 40 cm and refractive index n = 1.
solution_steps: Recall formula for longitudinal mode spacing: \Delta\nu = \frac{c}{2nL}.
Identify given values: c = 3 \times 10^8 \text{ m/s}, n = 1, L = 0.4 \text{ m}.

assumptions_and_limitations: Einstein's relations assume a simple two-level or three-level atomic system interacting with isotropic blackbody radiation.
Laser threshold equations assume steady-state conditions and uniform gain distribution across the optical cavity mode volume.

common_misconceptions.correct: Spontaneous emission produces incoherent light with random phase.
common_misconceptions.why: Independent atoms emit photons independently without phase coordination in spontaneous emission.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Population inversion can be achieved in a two-level system using optical pumping.
common_misconceptions.correct: Population inversion is impossible in a two-level system under steady-state optical pumping.
common_misconceptions.why: Pumping rates cannot exceed stimulated emission rates in a two-level system, capping the population ratio at 1:1.

quick_revision: LASER requires population inversion, stimulated emission, and an optical feedback cavity.
Four-level lasers are more efficient than three-level lasers because the lower laser level empties rapidly via non-radiative decay.
